section_1.title: The Hook: Order from Chaos
section_1.content: Introduce the paradoxical idea that while individual events are unpredictable, the average of those events follows a strict, predictable pattern. Use a visual metaphor of a 'Galton Board' (Quincunx) to show randomness turning into a Bell Curve.
section_1.example: Imagine thousands of tiny digital 'Space Rabbits' hopping randomly left or right. Individually, we can't guess where one rabbit lands. But when we look at the average position of groups of rabbits, a perfect 'Bell Shape' always emerges.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Establish the foundational vocabulary. Define the 'Population' (the entire group) and 'Samples' (small subsets). Explain the concept of 'Mean' (average) and 'Distribution' (the shape of the data).
section_2.example: Visualize a 'Cookie Factory' with a giant vat of dough (Population). The individual cookies we bake are 'Samples.' Some cookies might have 5 chocolate chips, others 15, creating a 'Distribution' of chip counts.

section_3.title: The Experiment: The Sampling Process
section_3.content: Demonstrate the core mechanic of the CLT: 1. Take a random sample of size 'n'. 2. Calculate its mean. 3. Repeat this 1,000 times. 4. Plot the distribution of those 1,000 means. Emphasize that we are graphing the 'Average of Averages'.
section_3.example: A robot named 'Data-Bot' picks 30 cookies at random, calculates their average weight, and marks it on a graph. Data-Bot repeats this process 500 times. The resulting graph is the 'Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean'.

section_4.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
section_4.content: The most critical point: Regardless of the original population's shape (skewed, uniform, or weird), the distribution of sample means will always become a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve) as the sample size 'n' increases (usually n ≥ 30).
section_4.example: Show a population distribution shaped like a 'Shark Fin' (highly skewed). As Data-Bot increases the sample size from n=2 to n=30, watch the 'Shark Fin' morph into a smooth, symmetrical 'Bell Curve' on the animation screen.

section_5.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
section_5.content: Introduce the properties of this new Bell Curve: 1. Its center (mean) is the same as the original population mean. 2. It becomes narrower (more precise) as the sample size 'n' increases. Introduce the formula for Standard Error: σ/√n.
section_5.example: If the average weight of all cookies in the factory is 50g, the center of our Bell Curve will be exactly at 50g. If we sample 100 cookies instead of 10, the 'Bell' becomes much skinnier and taller, showing higher precision.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Why It Matters
section_6.content: Explain that the CLT is the 'Powerhouse of Statistics' because it allows us to make inferences about any population using Normal Distribution math, even if the population itself isn't normal.
section_6.example: An engineer tests 50 lightbulbs from a batch of 1 million. Because of the CLT, she can use the Bell Curve to calculate the exact probability that the entire batch meets quality standards without testing every single bulb.

section_1.title: The Hook: Order from Chaos
section_1.content: Introduce the paradoxical idea that while individual events are unpredictable, the average of those events follows a strict, predictable pattern. Use a visual metaphor of a 'Galton Board' (Quincunx) to show randomness turning into a Bell Curve.
section_1.example: Imagine thousands of tiny digital 'Space Rabbits' hopping randomly left or right. Individually, we can't guess where one rabbit lands. But when we look at the average position of groups of rabbits, a perfect 'Bell Shape' always emerges.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Establish the foundational vocabulary. Define the 'Population' (the entire group) and 'Samples' (small subsets). Explain the concept of 'Mean' (average) and 'Distribution' (the shape of the data).
section_2.example: Visualize a 'Cookie Factory' with a giant vat of dough (Population). The individual cookies we bake are 'Samples.' Some cookies might have 5 chocolate chips, others 15, creating a 'Distribution' of chip counts.

section_3.title: The Experiment: The Sampling Process
section_3.content: Demonstrate the core mechanic of the CLT: 1. Take a random sample of size 'n'. 2. Calculate its mean. 3. Repeat this 1,000 times. 4. Plot the distribution of those 1,000 means. Emphasize that we are graphing the 'Average of Averages'.
section_3.example: A robot named 'Data-Bot' picks 30 cookies at random, calculates their average weight, and marks it on a graph. Data-Bot repeats this process 500 times. The resulting graph is the 'Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean'.

section_4.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
section_4.content: The most critical point: Regardless of the original population's shape (skewed, uniform, or weird), the distribution of sample means will always become a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve) as the sample size 'n' increases (usually n ≥ 30).
section_4.example: Show a population distribution shaped like a 'Shark Fin' (highly skewed). As Data-Bot increases the sample size from n=2 to n=30, watch the 'Shark Fin' morph into a smooth, symmetrical 'Bell Curve' on the animation screen.

section_5.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
section_5.content: Introduce the properties of this new Bell Curve: 1. Its center (mean) is the same as the original population mean. 2. It becomes narrower (more precise) as the sample size 'n' increases. Introduce the formula for Standard Error: σ/√n.
section_5.example: If the average weight of all cookies in the factory is 50g, the center of our Bell Curve will be exactly at 50g. If we sample 100 cookies instead of 10, the 'Bell' becomes much skinnier and taller, showing higher precision.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Why It Matters
section_6.content: Explain that the CLT is the 'Powerhouse of Statistics' because it allows us to make inferences about any population using Normal Distribution math, even if the population itself isn't normal.
section_6.example: An engineer tests 50 lightbulbs from a batch of 1 million. Because of the CLT, she can use the Bell Curve to calculate the exact probability that the entire batch meets quality standards without testing every single bulb.

lecture_lines: Individual events are often unpredictable and chaotic.

This creates order from chaos, forming a bell curve.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Population vs. Sample
lecture_lines: A population represents the entire group we study.
Samples are smaller subsets taken from that population.
Distribution describes the shape and spread of data.

section_3.title: The Experiment: The Sampling Process
lecture_lines: First, we take a random sample of size n.
Next, we calculate the average for that sample.
We repeat this process hundreds or thousands of times.
Each sample mean is plotted on a new graph.
This builds the sampling distribution of the mean.
animations: Highlight a random group of dots from a source to represent 'Sample size n'.
A yellow (#FFFF00) calculation 'Average =...' flashes above the selected dots.
The 'Average' value transforms into a single dot and drops onto a white (#FFFFFF) horizontal axis.
The process repeats rapidly 1000 times, showing many dots dropping.
The dots stack up to form the 'Sampling Distribution' shape.

section_4.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
lecture_lines: Start with any population shape, even highly skewed ones.
As sample size n increases, something magical happens.
The distribution of sample means begins to shift shape.
It always settles into a symmetrical normal distribution.
This is the core of the Central Limit Theorem.
animations: Display a magenta (#FF00FF) skewed 'Shark Fin' distribution labeled 'Population'.
Show a gray (#AAAAAA) jagged plot of sample means for a small sample size 'n=2'.
The value 'n=30' appears in white (#FFFFFF), and the jagged plot begins to smooth out.
The plot morphs into a symmetrical cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve.
White (#FFFFFF) text 'Central Limit Theorem' and green (#00FF00) 'Normal Distribution' appear as final labels.

section_5.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
lecture_lines: The sample mean's center matches the original population mean.
As n grows, the bell curve becomes much narrower.
This narrowing is called the standard error.
Formula: standard deviation divided by square root of n.
Larger samples provide much more precise estimates.
animations: Overlay an orange (#FF8C00) population curve and a cyan (#00FFFF) sample mean curve.
A white (#FFFFFF) vertical dashed line appears, aligning the peaks of both curves at 'Mean = mu'.
Animate the cyan curve narrowing and becoming taller as a white 'n' value increases.
The yellow (#FFFF00) formula 'SE = sigma / sqrt(n)' appears next to the narrow curve.
A horizontal arrow indicates the width (Standard Error) shrinking as 'n' grows larger.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Why It Matters
lecture_lines: The CLT is the powerhouse of modern statistics.
We can study any population using normal distribution math.
This allows for accurate predictions from small samples.
animations: Show a khaki (#F0E68C) box representing '1 Million Lightbulbs'.
Pull out a small cluster of 50 bulbs and draw a cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve over them.
A green (#00FF00) arrow labeled 'Inference' points from the small curve back to the large box.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout(
            "The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property", 
            [
                "Start with any population shape, even highly skewed ones.",
                "As sample size n increases, something magical happens.",
                "The distribution of sample means begins to shift shape.",
                "It always settles into a symmetrical normal distribution.",
                "This is the core of the Central Limit Theorem."
            ]
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(MAGENTA)
        
        # Shark Fin Population Shape
        shark_fin = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: 4 * x * np.exp(-x),
            x_range=[0, 4],
            color=MAGENTA
        )
        self.place_in_area(shark_fin, "A4", "B6", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        pop_label = Text("Population", font_size=18, color=MAGENTA)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A3", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(Create(shark_fin), Write(pop_label))
        self.wait(1)

        self.lecture[1].set_color(GRAY)

        ]

        n_label = Text("n = 2", font_size=20, color=WHITE)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # n increases to 30
        n30_label = Text("n = 30", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(n30_label, "D2", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Slightly smoother but still somewhat jagged version
        medium_points = [
            [-2, 0, 0], [-1.2, 0.4, 0], [-0.6, 1.2, 0], [0, 1.5, 0], 
            [0.6, 1.2, 0], [1.2, 0.4, 0], [2, 0, 0]
        ]
        medium_plot = VMobject(color=GRAY_A).set_points_smoothly([np.array(p) for p in medium_points])

        # Smooth Bell Curve

            lambda x: 2 * np.exp(-x**2),
            x_range=[-2, 2],
            color=CYAN
        )
        self.place_in_area(bell_curve, "D3", "F6", scale_factor=0.8)
        
        self.play(Transform(jagged_plot, bell_curve))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(GREEN)
        
        clt_text = Text("Central Limit Theorem", font_size=22, color=WHITE)

    def construct(self):
        # Setup the layout with title and lecture lines
        self.setup_layout(
            "Real-World Application: Why It Matters",
            [
                "The CLT is the powerhouse of modern statistics.",
                "We can study any population using normal distribution math.",
                "This allows for accurate predictions from small samples."
            ]
        )
        
        KHAKI = "#F0E68C"
        CYAN = "#00FFFF"
        GREEN = "#00FF00"

        self.place_in_area(large_box, 'B1', 'D3')
        self.place_at_grid(box_label, 'A2')
        
        # Add many small dots inside the box to represent bulbs
        np.random.seed(42)
        bulbs_in_box = VGroup(*[
            Dot(point=large_box.get_center() + np.array([
                np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0),
                np.random.uniform(-0.8, 0.8),
                0
            ]), radius=0.03, color=KHAKI)
            for _ in range(100)
        ])

            Create(large_box),
            Write(box_label),

        )

        self.lecture[1].set_color(CYAN)

        for _ in range(50):

            sample_group.add(dot)
        sample_group.arrange_in_grid(rows=5, cols=10, buff=0.05)
        
        # Move sample group to area E4 to F5
        self.place_in_area(sample_group, 'E4', 'F6', scale_factor=0.6)
        sample_label = Text("Sample: 50 Bulbs", font_size=16, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_label, 'D5')

        # Normal distribution curve (bell curve)
        ax = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3],
            y_range=[0, 1],
            x_length=2,
            y_length=1.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "include_ticks": False}
        ).set_color(CYAN)
        
        curve = ax.plot(
            lambda x: np.exp(-x**2),
            color=CYAN
        )
        bell_curve_group = VGroup(ax, curve)
        self.place_in_area(bell_curve_group, 'E4', 'F6', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Animation: Pulling bulbs from the box to the sample area
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(bulbs_in_box[:10].copy(), sample_group),
            Write(sample_label)
        )
        self.play(Create(bell_curve_group))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # A green (#00FF00) arrow labeled 'Inference' points from the small curve back to the large box.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN)
        
        inference_arrow = Arrow(
            start=self.grid['D5'],
            end=self.grid['D2'],
            color=GREEN,
            buff=0.1
        )
        inference_label = Text("Inference", font_size=20, color=GREEN)
        # Position label near the middle of the arrow
        inference_label.next_to(inference_arrow, RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(
            GrowArrow(inference_arrow),
            Write(inference_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # Clean up colors
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

            "Each sample mean is plotted on a new graph.",
            "This builds the sampling distribution of the mean."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Experiment: The Sampling Process", lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_SAMPLE = BLUE_B
        COLOR_AVG = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_AXIS = WHITE
        COLOR_POP = GREY_B

        # 1. Background Setup: Source Population
        population = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.04, color=COLOR_POP) for _ in range(80)])
        population.arrange_in_grid(rows=8, cols=10, buff=0.15)
        self.place_in_area(population, "A2", "B5", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.add(population)

        pop_label = Text("Source Population", font_size=16, color=COLOR_POP)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A1", scale_factor=0.8)

        # 2. Setup Axis for Distribution
        axis = NumberLine(
            x_range=[0, 10, 1],
            length=5,
            color=COLOR_AXIS,
            include_numbers=False,
            include_tip=True
        )
        self.place_in_area(axis, "F2", "F5", scale_factor=1.0)

        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Select n random dots from population to highlight

        highlighted_dots = VGroup(*[population[i] for i in sample_indices])
        
        sample_box = SurroundingRectangle(highlighted_dots, color=COLOR_SAMPLE, buff=0.1)
        sample_label = Text("n=15", font_size=18, color=COLOR_SAMPLE).next_to(sample_box, RIGHT)

            highlighted_dots.animate.set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE).scale(1.3),
            Create(sample_box),
            Write(sample_label),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Next, we calculate the average for that sample.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_AVG)
        
        avg_text = MathTex(r"\text{Average} = \bar{x}", color=COLOR_AVG, font_size=32)
        self.place_at_grid(avg_text, "C3", scale_factor=1.0)

        self.play(Indicate(avg_text, color=COLOR_AVG), run_time=1)
        self.wait(0.5)

        # (Plotting first mean)
        # Each sample mean is plotted on a new graph.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_AVG)
        
        first_mean_val = 5.2
        first_dot = Dot(color=COLOR_AVG, radius=0.06).move_to(axis.n2p(first_mean_val))
        
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(avg_text.copy(), first_dot),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # We repeat this process hundreds or thousands of times.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Clean up labels for repeat animation
        self.play(FadeOut(sample_box), FadeOut(sample_label), FadeOut(avg_text))
        
        # Repeated samples appearing and transforming into dots
        for _ in range(4):
            # Flash a new sample
            new_indices = np.random.choice(len(population), 15, replace=False)
            new_sample = VGroup(*[population[i].copy().set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE).scale(1.3) for i in new_indices])
            new_val = np.random.normal(5, 0.7)
            new_dot = Dot(color=COLOR_AVG, radius=0.06).move_to(axis.n2p(new_val))
            
            self.play(
                FadeIn(new_sample, run_time=0.2),
                ReplacementTransform(new_sample, new_dot, run_time=0.4),
            )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This builds the sampling distribution of the mean.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Massive drop of dots
        remaining_dots = VGroup()
        n_dots = 120
        # Calculate positions in a bell curve shape
        bins = np.zeros(20)
        for _ in range(n_dots):
            val = np.random.normal(5, 0.7)
            # Find bin
            bin_idx = int(np.clip((val - 2) * 4, 0, 19))
            height = bins[bin_idx]
            bins[bin_idx] += 1
            
            dot_pos = axis.n2p(2 + bin_idx/4) + UP * (height * 0.1)
            dot = Dot(color=COLOR_AVG, radius=0.04, fill_opacity=0.8).move_to(dot_pos)
            remaining_dots.add(dot)
            
        self.play(
            LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(d) for d in remaining_dots], lag_ratio=0.02),
            run_time=3
        )
        
        # Final normal distribution curve
        dist_curve = axis.get_graph(
            lambda x: 1.5 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - 5) / 0.7)**2),
            color=WHITE,
            x_range=[2.5, 7.5]
        )
        self.play(Create(dist_curve), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(2)

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Individual events are often unpredictable and chaotic.",
            "But groups of events follow strict, predictable patterns.",
            "This creates order from chaos, forming a bell curve."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Hook: Order from Chaos", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Highlight Line 1 in Yellow to match the Space Rabbits
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFD700")
        
        # Show many yellow dots ('Space Rabbits') moving randomly
        num_dots = 45
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#FFD700", radius=0.07) for _ in range(num_dots)])
        
        # Get boundaries from grid system for initial distribution
        tl = self.grid["A1"]
        br = self.grid["D6"]
        
        for dot in dots:
            dot.move_to([
                np.random.uniform(tl[0], br[0]),
                np.random.uniform(br[1], tl[1]),
                0
            ])
        
        self.add(dots)
        
        # Define jitter movement using an updater for efficiency
        def jitter_dots(d, dt):
            # Move dots slightly in a random direction to simulate chaos
            d.shift(np.array([np.random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2), np.random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2), 0]))
            # Maintain dots within the upper grid area (A1-D6)
            if d.get_x() < tl[0]: d.set_x(tl[0])
            if d.get_x() > br[0]: d.set_x(br[0])
            if d.get_y() < br[1]: d.set_y(br[1])
            if d.get_y() > tl[1]: d.set_y(tl[1])

        for dot in dots:
            dot.add_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        self.wait(3)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Reset line 1 color and highlight line 2 in white
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        
        # White horizontal axis appears at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"] + LEFT*0.5, self.grid["F6"] + RIGHT*0.5, color=WHITE)
        self.play(Create(axis))
        
        # Dots stop jittering and move to form stacks
        # Using a binomial distribution (n=5, p=0.5) to simulate the Galton board outcome
        for dot in dots:
            dot.remove_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        bins = [[] for _ in range(6)]
        for dot in dots:
            bin_idx = np.random.binomial(5, 0.5)
            bins[bin_idx].append(dot)
            
        stack_anims = []
        for col_idx in range(6):
            col_key = str(col_idx + 1)
            base_pos = self.grid[f"F{col_key}"]
            for stack_idx, dot in enumerate(bins[col_idx]):
                # Stack dots vertically on the axis at each grid column
                target = base_pos + UP * (0.15 + stack_idx * 0.16)
                stack_anims.append(dot.animate.move_to(target))
                
        self.play(*stack_anims, run_time=3)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Reset line 2 and highlight line 3 in Cyan
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        
        # A cyan bell curve outline fades in over the accumulated stacks
        # Center the curve based on the bin distribution (between col 3 and 4)
        center_x = (self.grid["F3"][0] + self.grid["F4"][0]) / 2
        baseline_y = self.grid["F1"][1]
        
        bell_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: 2.3 * np.exp(-((x - center_x)**2) / 1.5) + baseline_y,
            x_range=[self.grid["F1"][0]-0.3, self.grid["F6"][0]+0.3],
            color="#00FFFF"
        )
        
        self.play(FadeIn(bell_curve))
        self.wait(4)

import numpy as np

        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "First, we take a random sample of size n.",
            "Next, we calculate the average for that sample.",
            "We repeat this process hundreds or thousands of times.",
            "Each sample mean is plotted on a new graph.",
            "This builds the sampling distribution of the mean."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Experiment: The Sampling Process", lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_SAMPLE = BLUE_B
        COLOR_AVG = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_AXIS = WHITE
        COLOR_POP = GREY_B

        # 1. Background Setup: Source Population
        population = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.04, color=COLOR_POP) for _ in range(80)])
        population.arrange_in_grid(rows=8, cols=10, buff=0.15)
        self.place_in_area(population, "A2", "B5", scale_factor=1.0)
        self.add(population)

        pop_label = Text("Source Population", font_size=16, color=COLOR_POP)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A1", scale_factor=0.8)

        # 2. Setup Axis for Distribution
        axis = NumberLine(
            x_range=[0, 10, 1],
            length=5,
            color=COLOR_AXIS,
            include_numbers=False,
            include_tip=True
        )
        self.place_in_area(axis, "F2", "F5", scale_factor=1.0)
        axis_label = Text("Sampling Distribution of the Mean", font_size=16, color=COLOR_AXIS)
        self.place_at_grid(axis_label, "E1", scale_factor=0.8)
        self.add(axis)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # First, we take a random sample of size n.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Select n random dots from population to highlight
        sample_indices = np.random.choice(len(population), 15, replace=False)
        highlighted_dots = VGroup(*[population[i] for i in sample_indices])
        
        sample_box = SurroundingRectangle(highlighted_dots, color=COLOR_SAMPLE, buff=0.1)
        sample_label = Text("n=15", font_size=18, color=COLOR_SAMPLE).next_to(sample_box, RIGHT)
        
        self.play(
            highlighted_dots.animate.set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE).scale(1.3),
            Create(sample_box),
            Write(sample_label),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Next, we calculate the average for that sample.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_AVG)
        
        avg_text = MathTex(r"\text{Average} = \bar{x}", color=COLOR_AVG, font_size=32)
        self.place_at_grid(avg_text, "C3", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(avg_text), run_time=0.8)
        self.play(Indicate(avg_text, color=COLOR_AVG), run_time=1)
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # (Plotting first mean)
        # Each sample mean is plotted on a new graph.
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_AVG)
        
        first_mean_val = 5.2
        first_dot = Dot(color=COLOR_AVG, radius=0.06).move_to(axis.n2p(first_mean_val))
        
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(avg_text.copy(), first_dot),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # We repeat this process hundreds or thousands of times.
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Clean up labels for repeat animation
        self.play(FadeOut(sample_box), FadeOut(sample_label), FadeOut(avg_text))
        
        # Repeated samples appearing and transforming into dots
        for _ in range(4):
            # Flash a new sample
            new_indices = np.random.choice(len(population), 15, replace=False)
            new_sample = VGroup(*[population[i].copy().set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE).scale(1.3) for i in new_indices])
            new_val = np.random.normal(5, 0.7)
            new_dot = Dot(color=COLOR_AVG, radius=0.06).move_to(axis.n2p(new_val))
            
            self.play(
                FadeIn(new_sample, run_time=0.2),
                ReplacementTransform(new_sample, new_dot, run_time=0.4),
            )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # This builds the sampling distribution of the mean.
        self.lecture[4].set_color(WHITE)
        
        # Massive drop of dots
        remaining_dots = VGroup()
        n_dots = 120
        # Calculate positions in a bell curve shape
        bins = np.zeros(20)
        for _ in range(n_dots):
            val = np.random.normal(5, 0.7)
            # Find bin
            bin_idx = int(np.clip((val - 2) * 4, 0, 19))
            height = bins[bin_idx]
            bins[bin_idx] += 1
            
            dot_pos = axis.n2p(2 + bin_idx/4) + UP * (height * 0.1)
            dot = Dot(color=COLOR_AVG, radius=0.04, fill_opacity=0.8).move_to(dot_pos)
            remaining_dots.add(dot)
            
        self.play(
            LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(d) for d in remaining_dots], lag_ratio=0.02),
            run_time=3
        )
        
        # Final normal distribution curve
        dist_curve = axis.get_graph(
            lambda x: 1.5 * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - 5) / 0.7)**2),
            color=WHITE,
            x_range=[2.5, 7.5]
        )
        self.play(Create(dist_curve), run_time=1.5)
        self.wait(2)

        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_POP = "#FF8C00" # Orange
        COLOR_SAMPLE = "#00FFFF" # Cyan
        COLOR_FORMULA = "#FFFF00" # Yellow
        COLOR_TEXT = "#FFFFFF" # White

        # Normal Distribution Function
        def normal_pdf(x, mu, sigma):
            return (1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))) * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma)**2)

        # White horizontal axis appears at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"] + LEFT*0.5, self.grid["F6"] + RIGHT*0.5, color=WHITE)
        self.play(Create(axis))
        
        # Dots stop jittering and move to form stacks
        # Using a binomial distribution (n=5, p=0.5) to simulate the Galton board outcome
        for dot in dots:
            dot.remove_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        bins = [[] for _ in range(6)]
        for dot in dots:
            bin_idx = np.random.binomial(5, 0.5)
            bins[bin_idx].append(dot)
            
        stack_anims = []
        for col_idx in range(6):
            col_key = str(col_idx + 1)
            base_pos = self.grid[f"F{col_key}"]
            for stack_idx, dot in enumerate(bins[col_idx]):
                # Stack dots vertically on the axis at each grid column
                target = base_pos + UP * (0.15 + stack_idx * 0.16)
                stack_anims.append(dot.animate.move_to(target))
                
        self.play(*stack_anims, run_time=3)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Reset line 2 and highlight line 3 in Cyan
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        
        # A cyan bell curve outline fades in over the accumulated stacks
        # Center the curve based on the bin distribution (between col 3 and 4)
        center_x = (self.grid["F3"][0] + self.grid["F4"][0]) / 2
        baseline_y = self.grid["F1"][1]
        
        bell_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: 2.3 * np.exp(-((x - center_x)**2) / 1.5) + baseline_y,
            x_range=[self.grid["F1"][0]-0.3, self.grid["F6"][0]+0.3],
            color="#00FFFF"
        )
        
        self.play(FadeIn(bell_curve))
        self.wait(4)

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(f"- {line}", font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (6x6 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1.0
                y = 2.2 - i * 1.0
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup
        title = "Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error"
        lines = [
            "The sample mean's center matches the original population mean.",
            "As n grows, the bell curve becomes much narrower.",
            "This narrowing is called the standard error.",
            "Formula: standard deviation divided by square root of n.",
            "Larger samples provide much more precise estimates."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_POP = "#FF8C00" # Orange
        COLOR_SAMPLE = "#00FFFF" # Cyan
        COLOR_FORMULA = "#FFFF00" # Yellow
        COLOR_TEXT = "#FFFFFF" # White

        # Normal Distribution Function
        def normal_pdf(x, mu, sigma):
            return (1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))) * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma)**2)

        # Base parameters
        mu = 0
        sigma_pop = 1.0
        n_tracker = ValueTracker(1)

        # Coordinate references
        # Center the distribution between col 3 and 4
        x_center = (self.grid["E3"][0] + self.grid["E4"][0]) / 2
        y_base = self.grid["E1"][1]

        # X-axis for reference
        x_axis = Line(
            start=self.grid["E1"] + LEFT * 0.2,
            end=self.grid["E6"] + RIGHT * 0.2,
            color=WHITE,
            stroke_width=2
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_POP)
        
        # Population Curve
        pop_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: normal_pdf(x, 0, sigma_pop),
            x_range=[-3, 3, 0.05],
            color=COLOR_POP
        )
        # Using move_to with aligned_edge to keep it on the x-axis
        pop_curve.move_to([x_center, y_base, 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)

        # Sample Mean Curve (initially same as pop)
        sample_curve = pop_curve.copy().set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)

        # Vertical dashed line at peaks
        peak_x = x_center
        peak_y_top = self.grid["A3"][1] + 0.5
        peak_y_bottom = y_base
        
        center_line = DashedLine(
            start=[peak_x, peak_y_bottom, 0],
            end=[peak_x, peak_y_top, 0],
            color=COLOR_TEXT
        )
        mu_label = MathTex(r"\mu", color=COLOR_TEXT, font_size=32)
        mu_label.next_to(center_line, UP, buff=0.1)

        self.add(x_axis)
        self.play(Create(pop_curve), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(sample_curve), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(center_line), Write(mu_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # n label
        n_label_text = Text("n = ", font_size=24, color=COLOR_TEXT)
        n_value = DecimalNumber(1, num_decimal_places=0, color=COLOR_TEXT, font_size=24)
        n_group = VGroup(n_label_text, n_value).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(n_group, "B5")

        n_value.add_updater(lambda d: d.set_value(n_tracker.get_value()))
        
        # Updater for cyan curve
        def update_sample_curve(mob):
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            if n_val < 1: n_val = 1
            sigma_sample = sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_val)
            # Limit precision/height to prevent performance hit and off-screen peaks
            # Max height at sigma=0.1 is ~4.0, which fits in our grid
            new_mob = FunctionGraph(
                lambda x: normal_pdf(x, 0, sigma_sample),
                x_range=[-3, 3, 0.02],
                color=COLOR_SAMPLE
            )
            new_mob.move_to([x_center, y_base, 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)
            mob.become(new_mob)

        sample_curve.add_updater(update_sample_curve)
        
        self.add(n_group)
        self.play(n_tracker.animate.set_value(16), run_time=2, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Indicator for width (Standard Error)
        def get_se_arrow():
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            sigma_se = sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_val)
            y_pos = y_base + 0.3
            # Arrow representing 1 sigma (Standard Error)
            arrow = DoubleArrow(
                start=[x_center, y_pos, 0],
                end=[x_center + sigma_se, y_pos, 0],
                buff=0,
                color=COLOR_TEXT,
                stroke_width=2,
                max_tip_length_to_length_ratio=0.2
            )
            return arrow

        se_arrow = always_redraw(get_se_arrow)
        se_text = Text("Standard Error", font_size=18, color=COLOR_TEXT)
        # Using updater for text position to follow the arrow
        se_text.add_updater(lambda t: t.next_to(se_arrow, UP, buff=0.05))
        
        self.play(Create(se_arrow), Write(se_text))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_FORMULA)
        
        formula = MathTex(
            r"SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}",
            color=COLOR_FORMULA,
            font_size=32
        )
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B2")
        
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_TEXT)
        
        # Show higher precision with even larger n
        self.play(
            n_tracker.animate.set_value(81),
            run_time=3,
            rate_func=smooth
        )
        self.wait(2)

section_1.title: The Hook: Order from Chaos
section_1.content: Introduce the paradoxical idea that while individual events are unpredictable, the average of those events follows a strict, predictable pattern. Use a visual metaphor of a 'Galton Board' (Quincunx) to show randomness turning into a Bell Curve.
section_1.example: Imagine thousands of tiny digital 'Space Rabbits' hopping randomly left or right. Individually, we can't guess where one rabbit lands. But when we look at the average position of groups of rabbits, a perfect 'Bell Shape' always emerges.

section_2.title: Prerequisite Knowledge: Population vs. Sample
section_2.content: Establish the foundational vocabulary. Define the 'Population' (the entire group) and 'Samples' (small subsets). Explain the concept of 'Mean' (average) and 'Distribution' (the shape of the data).
section_2.example: Visualize a 'Cookie Factory' with a giant vat of dough (Population). The individual cookies we bake are 'Samples.' Some cookies might have 5 chocolate chips, others 15, creating a 'Distribution' of chip counts.

section_3.title: The Experiment: The Sampling Process
section_3.content: Demonstrate the core mechanic of the CLT: 1. Take a random sample of size 'n'. 2. Calculate its mean. 3. Repeat this 1,000 times. 4. Plot the distribution of those 1,000 means. Emphasize that we are graphing the 'Average of Averages'.
section_3.example: A robot named 'Data-Bot' picks 30 cookies at random, calculates their average weight, and marks it on a graph. Data-Bot repeats this process 500 times. The resulting graph is the 'Sampling Distribution of the Sample Mean'.

section_4.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
section_4.content: The most critical point: Regardless of the original population's shape (skewed, uniform, or weird), the distribution of sample means will always become a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve) as the sample size 'n' increases (usually n ≥ 30).
section_4.example: Show a population distribution shaped like a 'Shark Fin' (highly skewed). As Data-Bot increases the sample size from n=2 to n=30, watch the 'Shark Fin' morph into a smooth, symmetrical 'Bell Curve' on the animation screen.

section_5.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
section_5.content: Introduce the properties of this new Bell Curve: 1. Its center (mean) is the same as the original population mean. 2. It becomes narrower (more precise) as the sample size 'n' increases. Introduce the formula for Standard Error: σ/√n.
section_5.example: If the average weight of all cookies in the factory is 50g, the center of our Bell Curve will be exactly at 50g. If we sample 100 cookies instead of 10, the 'Bell' becomes much skinnier and taller, showing higher precision.

section_6.title: Real-World Application: Why It Matters
section_6.content: Explain that the CLT is the 'Powerhouse of Statistics' because it allows us to make inferences about any population using Normal Distribution math, even if the population itself isn't normal.
section_6.example: An engineer tests 50 lightbulbs from a batch of 1 million. Because of the CLT, she can use the Bell Curve to calculate the exact probability that the entire batch meets quality standards without testing every single bulb.

import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE

        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1

        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Individual events are often unpredictable and chaotic.",
            "But groups of events follow strict, predictable patterns.",
            "This creates order from chaos, forming a bell curve."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Hook: Order from Chaos", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Highlight Line 1 in Yellow to match the Space Rabbits
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFD700")
        
        # Show many yellow dots ('Space Rabbits') moving randomly
        num_dots = 45
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#FFD700", radius=0.07) for _ in range(num_dots)])
        
        # Get boundaries from grid system for initial distribution
        tl = self.grid["A1"]
        br = self.grid["D6"]
        
        for dot in dots:
            dot.move_to([
                np.random.uniform(tl[0], br[0]),
                np.random.uniform(br[1], tl[1]),
                0
            ])
        
        self.add(dots)
        
        # Define jitter movement using an updater for efficiency
        def jitter_dots(d, dt):
            # Move dots slightly in a random direction to simulate chaos
            d.shift(np.array([np.random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2), np.random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2), 0]))
            # Maintain dots within the upper grid area (A1-D6)
            if d.get_x() < tl[0]: d.set_x(tl[0])
            if d.get_x() > br[0]: d.set_x(br[0])
            if d.get_y() < br[1]: d.set_y(br[1])
            if d.get_y() > tl[1]: d.set_y(tl[1])

        for dot in dots:
            dot.add_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        self.wait(3)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Reset line 1 color and highlight line 2 in white
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        
        # White horizontal axis appears at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"] + LEFT*0.5, self.grid["F6"] + RIGHT*0.5, color=WHITE)
        self.play(Create(axis))
        
        # Dots stop jittering and move to form stacks
        # Using a binomial distribution (n=5, p=0.5) to simulate the Galton board outcome
        for dot in dots:
            dot.remove_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        bins = [[] for _ in range(6)]
        for dot in dots:
            bin_idx = np.random.binomial(5, 0.5)
            bins[bin_idx].append(dot)
            
        stack_anims = []
        for col_idx in range(6):
            col_key = str(col_idx + 1)
            base_pos = self.grid[f"F{col_key}"]
            for stack_idx, dot in enumerate(bins[col_idx]):
                # Stack dots vertically on the axis at each grid column
                target = base_pos + UP * (0.15 + stack_idx * 0.16)
                stack_anims.append(dot.animate.move_to(target))
                
        self.play(*stack_anims, run_time=3)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Reset line 2 and highlight line 3 in Cyan
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        
        # A cyan bell curve outline fades in over the accumulated stacks
        # Center the curve based on the bin distribution (between col 3 and 4)
        center_x = (self.grid["F3"][0] + self.grid["F4"][0]) / 2
        baseline_y = self.grid["F1"][1]
        
        bell_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: 2.3 * np.exp(-((x - center_x)**2) / 1.5) + baseline_y,
            x_range=[self.grid["F1"][0]-0.3, self.grid["F6"][0]+0.3],
            color="#00FFFF"
        )
        
        self.play(FadeIn(bell_curve))
        self.wait(4)

class Section3Scene(Scene):
    def construct(self):
        # 1. Setup Layout
        title = Text("The Central Limit Theorem (CLT)", font_size=32, color=BLUE).to_edge(UP)
        
        lecture_lines = [
            "1. Take samples from ANY distribution.",
            "2. Calculate the average of each sample.",
            "3. The distribution of these averages...",
            "4. ...will always be Normal (Bell Curve)!"
        ]
        
        lecture_vgroup = VGroup(*[
            Text(line, font_size=20).arrange(RIGHT, aligned_edge=LEFT) 
            for line in lecture_lines
        ]).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT, buff=0.4).to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.5).shift(DOWN*0.5)

        self.play(Write(title))
        self.play(FadeIn(lecture_vgroup, shift=RIGHT))
        self.wait(1)

        # 2. Visual Representation Area (Right Side)
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[0, 10, 2],
            y_range=[0, 1, 0.5],
            x_length=5,
            y_length=3,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "font_size": 18}
        ).to_edge(RIGHT, buff=0.8).shift(UP*0.5)
        
        labels = axes.get_axis_labels(x_label="Value", y_label="Prob")
        
        # Original Distribution: Uniform
        uniform_dist = axes.plot(lambda x: 0.2 if 1 <= x <= 9 else 0, color=YELLOW, x_range=[0, 10])
        dist_label = Text("Uniform Distribution", font_size=18, color=YELLOW).next_to(axes, DOWN)

        self.play(Create(axes), Write(labels))
        self.play(Create(uniform_dist), Write(dist_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # 3. Sampling Animation
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(axes.c2p(np.random.uniform(1, 9), 0.2), color=WHITE, radius=0.04) for _ in range(20)])
        sample_text = Text("Sampling...", font_size=18).next_to(dist_label, DOWN)
        
        self.play(Write(sample_text))
        self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(dot) for dot in dots], lag_ratio=0.05))
        self.play(FadeOut(dots), FadeOut(uniform_dist), FadeOut(dist_label))

        # 4. Final Result: Normal Distribution
        # The CLT states that the distribution of means approaches a normal distribution
        mu = 5
        sigma = 1.2
        normal_dist = axes.plot(
            lambda x: (1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))) * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma)**2),
            color=GREEN,
            x_range=[0, 10]
        )
        result_label = Text("Distribution of Sample Means (Normal)", font_size=18, color=GREEN).next_to(axes, DOWN)

        self.play(Create(normal_dist), Write(result_label))
        self.play(Indicate(lecture_vgroup[-1], color=GREEN))
        self.wait(2)

        # Cleanup
        self.play(
            FadeOut(title),
            FadeOut(lecture_vgroup),
            FadeOut(axes),
            FadeOut(labels),
            FadeOut(normal_dist),
            FadeOut(result_label),
            FadeOut(sample_text)
        )

        # Colors
        COLOR_POP = "#FF8C00" # Orange
        COLOR_SAMPLE = "#00FFFF" # Cyan
        COLOR_FORMULA = "#FFFF00" # Yellow
        COLOR_TEXT = "#FFFFFF" # White

        # Normal Distribution Function
        def normal_pdf(x, mu, sigma):
            return (1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))) * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma)**2)

        # Base parameters
        mu = 0
        sigma_pop = 1.0
        n_tracker = ValueTracker(1)

        # Coordinate references
        # Center the distribution between col 3 and 4
        x_center = (self.grid["E3"][0] + self.grid["E4"][0]) / 2
        y_base = self.grid["E1"][1]

        # X-axis for reference
        x_axis = Line(
            start=self.grid["E1"] + LEFT * 0.2,
            end=self.grid["E6"] + RIGHT * 0.2,
            color=WHITE,
            stroke_width=2
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_POP)
        
        # Population Curve
        pop_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: normal_pdf(x, 0, sigma_pop),
            x_range=[-3, 3, 0.05],
            color=COLOR_POP
        )
        # Using move_to with aligned_edge to keep it on the x-axis
        pop_curve.move_to([x_center, y_base, 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)

        # Sample Mean Curve (initially same as pop)
        sample_curve = pop_curve.copy().set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)

        # Vertical dashed line at peaks
        peak_x = x_center
        peak_y_top = self.grid["A3"][1] + 0.5
        peak_y_bottom = y_base
        
        center_line = DashedLine(
            start=[peak_x, peak_y_bottom, 0],
            end=[peak_x, peak_y_top, 0],
            color=COLOR_TEXT
        )
        mu_label = MathTex(r"\mu", color=COLOR_TEXT, font_size=32)
        mu_label.next_to(center_line, UP, buff=0.1)

        self.add(x_axis)
        self.play(Create(pop_curve), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(sample_curve), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(center_line), Write(mu_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # n label
        n_label_text = Text("n = ", font_size=24, color=COLOR_TEXT)
        n_value = DecimalNumber(1, num_decimal_places=0, color=COLOR_TEXT, font_size=24)
        n_group = VGroup(n_label_text, n_value).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(n_group, "B5")

        n_value.add_updater(lambda d: d.set_value(n_tracker.get_value()))
        
        # Updater for cyan curve
        def update_sample_curve(mob):
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            if n_val < 1: n_val = 1
            sigma_sample = sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_val)
            # Limit precision/height to prevent performance hit and off-screen peaks
            # Max height at sigma=0.1 is ~4.0, which fits in our grid
            new_mob = FunctionGraph(
                lambda x: normal_pdf(x, 0, sigma_sample),
                x_range=[-3, 3, 0.02],
                color=COLOR_SAMPLE
            )
            new_mob.move_to([x_center, y_base, 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)
            mob.become(new_mob)

        sample_curve.add_updater(update_sample_curve)
        
        self.add(n_group)
        self.play(n_tracker.animate.set_value(16), run_time=2, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Indicator for width (Standard Error)
        def get_se_arrow():
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            sigma_se = sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_val)
            y_pos = y_base + 0.3
            # Arrow representing 1 sigma (Standard Error)
            arrow = DoubleArrow(
                start=[x_center, y_pos, 0],
                end=[x_center + sigma_se, y_pos, 0],
                buff=0,
                color=COLOR_TEXT,
                stroke_width=2,
                max_tip_length_to_length_ratio=0.2
            )
            return arrow

        se_arrow = always_redraw(get_se_arrow)
        se_text = Text("Standard Error", font_size=18, color=COLOR_TEXT)
        # Using updater for text position to follow the arrow
        se_text.add_updater(lambda t: t.next_to(se_arrow, UP, buff=0.05))
        
        self.play(Create(se_arrow), Write(se_text))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_FORMULA)
        
        formula = MathTex(
            r"SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}",
            color=COLOR_FORMULA,
            font_size=32
        )
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B2")
        
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_TEXT)
        
        # Show higher precision with even larger n
        self.play(
            n_tracker.animate.set_value(81),
            run_time=3,
            rate_func=smooth
        )
        self.wait(2)

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section6Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup the layout with title and lecture lines
        self.setup_layout(
            "Real-World Application: Why It Matters",
            [
                "The CLT is the powerhouse of modern statistics.",
                "We can study any population using normal distribution math.",
                "This allows for accurate predictions from small samples."
            ]
        )
        
        KHAKI = "#F0E68C"
        CYAN = "#00FFFF"
        GREEN = "#00FF00"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Show a khaki (#F0E68C) box representing '1 Million Lightbulbs'.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(KHAKI)
        
        large_box = Rectangle(width=2.5, height=2, color=KHAKI, fill_opacity=0.2)
        box_label = Text("1 Million Lightbulbs", font_size=18, color=KHAKI)
        
        # Place box in upper-center-right area
        self.place_in_area(large_box, 'B1', 'D3')
        self.place_at_grid(box_label, 'A2')
        
        # Add many small dots inside the box to represent bulbs
        np.random.seed(42)
        bulbs_in_box = VGroup(*[
            Dot(point=large_box.get_center() + np.array([
                np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0),
                np.random.uniform(-0.8, 0.8),
                0
            ]), radius=0.03, color=KHAKI)
            for _ in range(100)
        ])

        self.play(
            Create(large_box),
            Write(box_label),
            FadeIn(bulbs_in_box)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Pull out a small cluster of 50 bulbs and draw a cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve over them.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(CYAN)
        
        # Create a small cluster
        sample_group = VGroup()
        for _ in range(50):
            dot = Dot(radius=0.03, color=KHAKI)
            sample_group.add(dot)
        sample_group.arrange_in_grid(rows=5, cols=10, buff=0.05)
        
        # Move sample group to area E4 to F6
        self.place_in_area(sample_group, 'E4', 'F6', scale_factor=0.6)
        sample_label = Text("Sample: 50 Bulbs", font_size=16, color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_label, 'D5')

        # Normal distribution curve (bell curve)
        ax = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3],
            y_range=[0, 1],
            x_length=2,
            y_length=1.5,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "include_ticks": False}
        ).set_color(CYAN)
        
        curve = ax.plot(
            lambda x: np.exp(-x**2),
            color=CYAN
        )
        bell_curve_group = VGroup(ax, curve)
        self.place_in_area(bell_curve_group, 'E4', 'F6', scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Animation: Pulling bulbs from the box to the sample area
        self.play(
            ReplacementTransform(bulbs_in_box[:10].copy(), sample_group),
            Write(sample_label)
        )
        self.play(Create(bell_curve_group))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # A green (#00FF00) arrow labeled 'Inference' points from the small curve back to the large box.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN)
        
        inference_arrow = Arrow(
            start=self.grid['D5'],
            end=self.grid['D2'],
            color=GREEN,
            buff=0.1
        )
        inference_label = Text("Inference", font_size=20, color=GREEN)
        # Position label near the middle of the arrow
        inference_label.next_to(inference_arrow, RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(
            GrowArrow(inference_arrow),
            Write(inference_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # Clean up colors
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

outline.title: The Hook: Order from Chaos
outline.content: Introduce the paradoxical idea that while individual events are unpredictable, the average of those events follows a strict, predictable pattern. Use a visual metaphor of a 'Galton Board' (Quincunx) to show randomness turning into a Bell Curve.
outline.example: Imagine thousands of tiny digital 'Space Rabbits' hopping randomly left or right. Individually, we can't guess where one rabbit lands. But when we look at the average position of groups of rabbits, a perfect 'Bell Shape' always emerges.

But groups of events follow strict, predictable patterns.
This creates order from chaos, forming a bell curve.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Individual events are often unpredictable and chaotic.",
            "But groups of events follow strict, predictable patterns.",
            "This creates order from chaos, forming a bell curve."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Hook: Order from Chaos", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Highlight Line 1 in Yellow to match the Space Rabbits
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFD700")
        
        # Show many yellow dots ('Space Rabbits') moving randomly
        num_dots = 45
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#FFD700", radius=0.07) for _ in range(num_dots)])
        
        # Get boundaries from grid system for initial distribution
        tl = self.grid["A1"]
        br = self.grid["D6"]
        
        for dot in dots:
            dot.move_to([
                np.random.uniform(tl[0], br[0]),
                np.random.uniform(br[1], tl[1]),
                0
            ])
        
        self.add(dots)
        
        # Define jitter movement using an updater for efficiency
        def jitter_dots(d, dt):
            # Move dots slightly in a random direction to simulate chaos
            d.shift(np.array([np.random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2), np.random.uniform(-0.2, 0.2), 0]))
            # Maintain dots within the upper grid area (A1-D6)
            if d.get_x() < tl[0]: d.set_x(tl[0])
            if d.get_x() > br[0]: d.set_x(br[0])
            if d.get_y() < br[1]: d.set_y(br[1])
            if d.get_y() > tl[1]: d.set_y(tl[1])

        for dot in dots:
            dot.add_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        self.wait(3)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Reset line 1 color and highlight line 2 in white
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        
        # White horizontal axis appears at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"] + LEFT*0.5, self.grid["F6"] + RIGHT*0.5, color=WHITE)
        self.play(Create(axis))
        
        # Dots stop jittering and move to form stacks
        # Using a binomial distribution (n=5, p=0.5) to simulate the Galton board outcome
        for dot in dots:
            dot.remove_updater(jitter_dots)
            
        bins = [[] for _ in range(6)]
        for dot in dots:
            bin_idx = np.random.binomial(5, 0.5)
            bins[bin_idx].append(dot)
            
        stack_anims = []
        for col_idx in range(6):
            col_key = str(col_idx + 1)
            base_pos = self.grid[f"F{col_key}"]
            for stack_idx, dot in enumerate(bins[col_idx]):
                # Stack dots vertically on the axis at each grid column
                target = base_pos + UP * (0.15 + stack_idx * 0.16)
                stack_anims.append(dot.animate.move_to(target))
                
        self.play(*stack_anims, run_time=3)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Reset line 2 and highlight line 3 in Cyan
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FFFF")
        
        # A cyan bell curve outline fades in over the accumulated stacks
        # Center the curve based on the bin distribution (between col 3 and 4)
        center_x = (self.grid["F3"][0] + self.grid["F4"][0]) / 2
        baseline_y = self.grid["F1"][1]
        
        bell_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: 2.3 * np.exp(-((x - center_x)**2) / 1.5) + baseline_y,
            x_range=[self.grid["F1"][0]-0.3, self.grid["F6"][0]+0.3],
            color="#00FFFF"
        )
        
        self.play(FadeIn(bell_curve))
        self.wait(4)

outline.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
outline.content: Introduce the properties of this new Bell Curve: 1. Its center (mean) is the same as the original population mean. 2. It becomes narrower (more precise) as the sample size 'n' increases. Introduce the formula for Standard Error: σ/√n.
outline.example: If the average weight of all cookies in the factory is 50g, the center of our Bell Curve will be exactly at 50g. If we sample 100 cookies instead of 10, the 'Bell' becomes much skinnier and taller, showing higher precision.

storyboard.title: Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error
lecture_lines: The sample mean's center matches the original population mean.
As n grows, the bell curve becomes much narrower.
This narrowing is called the standard error.
Formula: standard deviation divided by square root of n.
Larger samples provide much more precise estimates.
animations: Overlay an orange (#FF8C00) population curve and a cyan (#00FFFF) sample mean curve.
A white (#FFFFFF) vertical dashed line appears, aligning the peaks of both curves at 'Mean = mu'.
Animate the cyan curve narrowing and becoming taller as a white 'n' value increases.
The yellow (#FFFF00) formula 'SE = sigma / sqrt(n)' appears next to the narrow curve.
A horizontal arrow indicates the width (Standard Error) shrinking as 'n' grows larger.

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup
        title = "Mathematical Nuance: Mean and Standard Error"
        lines = [
            "The sample mean's center matches the original population mean.",
            "As n grows, the bell curve becomes much narrower.",
            "This narrowing is called the standard error.",
            "Formula: standard deviation divided by square root of n.",
            "Larger samples provide much more precise estimates."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title, lines)

        # Colors
        COLOR_POP = "#FF8C00" # Orange
        COLOR_SAMPLE = "#00FFFF" # Cyan
        COLOR_FORMULA = "#FFFF00" # Yellow
        COLOR_TEXT = "#FFFFFF" # White

        # Normal Distribution Function
        def normal_pdf(x, mu, sigma):
            return (1 / (sigma * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))) * np.exp(-0.5 * ((x - mu) / sigma)**2)

        # Base parameters
        mu = 0
        sigma_pop = 1.0
        n_tracker = ValueTracker(1)

        # Coordinate references
        # Center the distribution between col 3 and 4
        x_center = (self.grid["E3"][0] + self.grid["E4"][0]) / 2
        y_base = self.grid["E1"][1]

        # X-axis for reference
        x_axis = Line(
            start=self.grid["E1"] + LEFT * 0.2,
            end=self.grid["E6"] + RIGHT * 0.2,
            color=WHITE,
            stroke_width=2
        )

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_POP)
        
        # Population Curve
        pop_curve = FunctionGraph(
            lambda x: normal_pdf(x, 0, sigma_pop),
            x_range=[-3, 3, 0.05],
            color=COLOR_POP
        )
        # Using move_to with aligned_edge to keep it on the x-axis
        pop_curve.move_to([x_center, y_base, 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)

        # Sample Mean Curve (initially same as pop)
        sample_curve = pop_curve.copy().set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)

        # Vertical dashed line at peaks
        peak_x = x_center
        peak_y_top = self.grid["A3"][1] + 0.5
        peak_y_bottom = y_base
        
        center_line = DashedLine(
            start=[peak_x, peak_y_bottom, 0],
            end=[peak_x, peak_y_top, 0],
            color=COLOR_TEXT
        )
        mu_label = MathTex(r"\mu", color=COLOR_TEXT, font_size=32)
        mu_label.next_to(center_line, UP, buff=0.1)

        self.add(x_axis)
        self.play(Create(pop_curve), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(sample_curve), run_time=1)
        self.play(Create(center_line), Write(mu_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # n label
        n_label_text = Text("n = ", font_size=24, color=COLOR_TEXT)
        n_value = DecimalNumber(1, num_decimal_places=0, color=COLOR_TEXT, font_size=24)
        n_group = VGroup(n_label_text, n_value).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(n_group, "B5")

        n_value.add_updater(lambda d: d.set_value(n_tracker.get_value()))
        
        # Updater for cyan curve
        def update_sample_curve(mob):
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            if n_val < 1: n_val = 1
            sigma_sample = sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_val)
            # Limit precision/height to prevent performance hit and off-screen peaks
            # Max height at sigma=0.1 is ~4.0, which fits in our grid
            new_mob = FunctionGraph(
                lambda x: normal_pdf(x, 0, sigma_sample),
                x_range=[-3, 3, 0.02],
                color=COLOR_SAMPLE
            )
            new_mob.move_to([x_center, y_base, 0], aligned_edge=DOWN)
            mob.become(new_mob)

        sample_curve.add_updater(update_sample_curve)
        
        self.add(n_group)
        self.play(n_tracker.animate.set_value(16), run_time=2, rate_func=linear)
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color(COLOR_SAMPLE)
        
        # Indicator for width (Standard Error)
        def get_se_arrow():
            n_val = n_tracker.get_value()
            sigma_se = sigma_pop / np.sqrt(n_val)
            y_pos = y_base + 0.3
            # Arrow representing 1 sigma (Standard Error)
            arrow = DoubleArrow(
                start=[x_center, y_pos, 0],
                end=[x_center + sigma_se, y_pos, 0],
                buff=0,
                color=COLOR_TEXT,
                stroke_width=2,
                max_tip_length_to_length_ratio=0.2
            )
            return arrow

        se_arrow = always_redraw(get_se_arrow)
        se_text = Text("Standard Error", font_size=18, color=COLOR_TEXT)
        # Using updater for text position to follow the arrow
        se_text.add_updater(lambda t: t.next_to(se_arrow, UP, buff=0.05))
        
        self.play(Create(se_arrow), Write(se_text))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color(COLOR_FORMULA)
        
        formula = MathTex(
            r"SE = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}",
            color=COLOR_FORMULA,
            font_size=32
        )
        self.place_at_grid(formula, "B2")
        
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color(COLOR_TEXT)
        
        # Show higher precision with even larger n
        self.play(
            n_tracker.animate.set_value(81),
            run_time=3,
            rate_func=smooth
        )
        self.wait(2)

outline.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
outline.content: The most critical point: Regardless of the original population's shape (skewed, uniform, or weird), the distribution of sample means will always become a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve) as the sample size 'n' increases (usually n ≥ 30).
outline.example: Show a population distribution shaped like a 'Shark Fin' (highly skewed). As Data-Bot increases the sample size from n=2 to n=30, watch the 'Shark Fin' morph into a smooth, symmetrical 'Bell Curve' on the animation screen.

storyboard.title: The Core Reveal: The Shape-Shifting Property
lecture_lines: Start with any population shape, even highly skewed ones.
As sample size n increases, something magical happens.
The distribution of sample means begins to shift shape.
It always settles into a symmetrical normal distribution.
This is the core of the Central Limit Theorem.
animations: Display a magenta (#FF00FF) skewed 'Shark Fin' [Asset: /scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/shark.svg] distribution labeled 'Population'.
Show a gray (#AAAAAA) jagged plot of sample means for a small sample size 'n=2'.
The value 'n=30' appears in white (#FFFFFF), and the jagged plot begins to smooth out.
The plot morphs into a symmetrical cyan (#00FFFF) bell curve.
White (#FFFFFF) text 'Central Limit Theorem' and green (#00FF00) 'Normal Distribution' appear as final labels.

from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

        jagged_points = [

        n_label = Text("n = 2", font_size=20, color=WHITE)

    def construct(self):
        # Setup the layout with title and lecture lines
        self.setup_layout(
            "Real-World Application: Why It Matters",
            [
                "The CLT is the powerhouse of modern statistics.",
                "We can study any population using normal distribution math.",
                "This allows for accurate predictions from small samples."
            ]
        )
        
        KHAKI = "#F0E68C"
        CYAN = "#00FFFF"
        GREEN = "#00FF00"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===

        self.lecture[0].set_color(KHAKI)
        
        large_box = Rectangle(width=2.5, height=2, color=KHAKI, fill_opacity=0.2)

        # Place box in upper-center-right area
        self.place_in_area(large_box, 'B1', 'D3')
        self.place_at_grid(box_label, 'A2')
        
        # Add many small dots inside the box to represent bulbs
        np.random.seed(42)
        bulbs_in_box = VGroup(*[
            Dot(point=large_box.get_center() + np.array([
                np.random.uniform(-1.0, 1.0),
                np.random.uniform(-0.8, 0.8),
                0
            ]), radius=0.03, color=KHAKI)
            for _ in range(100)

            Write(box_label),
            FadeIn(bulbs_in_box)

            y_length=1.5,

            ReplacementTransform(bulbs_in_box[:10].copy(), sample_group),
            Write(sample_label)
        )

        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===

        self.lecture[2].set_color(GREEN)
        
        inference_arrow = Arrow(
            start=self.grid['D5'],
            end=self.grid['D2'],
            color=GREEN,
            buff=0.1
        )
        inference_label = Text("Inference", font_size=20, color=GREEN)
        # Position label near the middle of the arrow

        self.play(
            GrowArrow(inference_arrow),
            Write(inference_label)
        )
        self.wait(2)

        # Clean up colors
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)
